paper_title: GameDojo: Benchmarking Real-Time Interactive Agents in Video Games

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Interactive intelligence requires agents to act on observations and adapt to the consequences of actions. Studying these abilities calls for diverse, challenging tasks under controlled conditions. We introduce GameDojo, a controllable interactive gameplay benchmark of 120 boss encounters across 20 games for evaluating model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses. Coding agents reconstruct the environments and write gameplay scripts, producing GameDojo-Data with 600 hours of gameplay trajectories. Experiments reveal substantial challenges for frontier models, especially in real-time interaction. Training on GameDojo-Data brings GameDojo-4B to frontier performance, with the strongest real-time performance. We also find joint training improves individual tasks, and learned policies transfer across bosses. Together, these findings establish GameDojo as a challenging and valuable interactive gameplay benchmark for the community. Our project page is at https://gamedojo-benchmark.github.io/ , and our code is at https://github.com/THUSI-Lab/GameDojo .

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Generalist agents must achieve goals through interaction with diverse environments (Reed et al., 2022; SIMA Team, 2024, 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026). This requires interactive intelligence: understanding the current situation, anticipating the consequences of actions, and continually adjusting decisions based on feedback (Yao et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026). Adversarial tasks concentrate these demands. An opponent continually changes the situation and opportunities for action, requiring agents to anticipate its behavior, choose response, and act at the right moment through precise control (Vinyals et al., 2019; de França et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026). These tasks provide concrete setting for examining how perception, prediction, decision-making, and control work together to produce effective behavior. Building diverse, repeatable adversarial tasks in the physical world is costly and can pose safety risks, making video games safe and controllable environment (Bellemare et al., 2013). However, whole-game evaluations combine navigation, puzzle solving, and combat (Zhang et al., 2025; Park et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c), making it difﬁcult to locate speciﬁc bottlenecks. Opensource environments often feature older or small games (Kempka et al., 2016; Cobbe et al., 2020), while modern games are typically closed-source (Tan et al., 2025b; Schuck, 2023). Implementing such encounters as independent environments preserves their interactive challenges while making task conditions controllable and outcomes measurable. We introduce GAMEDOJO, challenging benchmark of 120 boss encounters across 20 popular and classic games, together with GAMEDOJO-Data and GAMEDOJO-4B. Gameplay controllers collect 600-hour trajectory dataset, GAMEDOJO-Data, where we train GAMEDOJO-4B. Built on Gymnasium, GAMEDOJO supports custom experiments and provides uniﬁed evaluation interface for studying model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses on interactive gameplay tasks. Our contributions are threefold: diverse, controllable and challenging benchmark for interactive intelligence. We introduce GAMEDOJO, with 120 boss encounters across 20 diverse game environments. Conﬁgurable mechanics, action interfaces, timing modes and difﬁculties support controlled studies of model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses. An efﬁcient and automated pipeline to collect high-quality gameplay dataset. We build pipeline in which coding agents read game source code and write the behavior-tree controllers to efﬁciently collect gameplay data in parallel. This produces GAMEDOJO-Data, with 600 hours of high-quality gameplay trajectories covering all 120 encounters at three difﬁculty levels, training generalist agents and specialist policy network. Extensive experiments on interactive performance, learning, and transfer. GPT-6.1-Sol wins only 4% of encounters at medium difﬁculty with time paused and 0% in real time. Our GAMEDOJO-4B approaches frontier performance and achieves the best in real-time. Joint training improves individual tasks, and learned skills generalize across bosses and games. These ﬁndings establish GAMEDOJO as challenging and valuable interactive gameplay benchmark for the community.

sections.title: GAMEDOJO Environments
sections.content: Figure 2: Overview of GAMEDOJO. (1) Human-selected games and bosses guide coding agents that build environments and behavior-tree controllers from videos, wikis, and mechanics descriptions. (2) Scripts, LLM agents, and policy networks interact through conﬁgurable action interfaces, timing modes, and difﬁculty settings. (3) Parallel rollouts produce high-quality GAMEDOJO-Data efﬁciently without any manual gameplay. (4) The suite supports learning from generalist models and training specialist policies from scratch. (5) Shared tasks evaluate model capabilities, algorithms, and agent harnesses.

sections.title: 3.1 Task Deﬁnition and Notation
sections.content: Each task starts at boss encounter, with the goal of defeating the boss. At decision step t, the environment renders its internal state st into visual observation ot. The agent selects an action at π( ot, ht) from its observation and optional history ht = (o0, a0, . . . , at1). The action interface executes at, and the environment advances to st+1 under the selected timing mode and renders the next observation. This loop requires the agent to recognize attack cues, anticipate the bosss behavior, and adjust its strategy and control in response to feedback of the boss and environment.

sections.title: 3.2 GAMEDOJO Construction
sections.content: GAMEDOJO contains 120 boss encounters across 20 environments: 10 environments and 60 encounters each in 2D and 3D. We select representative games and bosses as references, covering the nine main interaction patterns in Table 2, from action platforming and bullet-hell dodging to ﬁrst-person shooting and racing. Differences in viewpoints, movement systems, and combat mechanics call for different strategies and forms of control. Table 1 compares benchmarks by environment count, task count, source availability, and core interactions. General game benchmarks combine navigation, puzzle solving, combat, and memory in broader tasks. The specialist adversarial environments in the table each focus on one interaction family in single game. GAMEDOJO uses individual boss encounters as common task unit across nine interaction patterns. For each selected reference game and boss in Table 2, we prepare the gameplay videos, wikis, and mechanics descriptions. The videos show attack cues, action timing, and phase changes; the wikis and mechanics descriptions detail hit rules, resource constraints, and other mechanics. sections.title: 3.3 Environment Details
sections.content: Each GAMEDOJO encounter is wrapped as Gym environment (Brockman et al., 2016) and uses ﬁxed rate of 60 Hz for both rendering and simulation ticks. The wrapper exposes reset() to start an episode and return the initial observation, and step(action) to apply an action and return the next observation, reward, and episode termination status. GAMEDOJO has the environment source code and can expose internal states, observations, controls, and mechanics parameters as needed, or customize resets, simulation timing, and rewards. In principle, GAMEDOJO enables developers to conduct any custom experiment. The standard GAMEDOJO evaluation uses two action interfaces, two timing modes, three difﬁculty settings, and common reward deﬁnition. Action interfaces. CUA accepts keyboard and mouse button presses and releases, as well as mouse movement. The model outputs structured action chunk at that the interface parses into low-level device commands (Tan et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2026). Each chunk covers 200 ms and uses the following format. at = <action_start> xt yt zt; (1) ; . . . ; (6) <action_end>, (1) where (xt, yt) [1000, 1000]2 are discretized relative mouse moves, zt [5, 5] is the scroll delta, and each contains 0-4 keys or mouse buttons held for 33 ms. (j) Semantic maps parameterized primitives such as movement, attacks, dodges, and skills to lowlevel controls. For example, the model can issue single 200 ms action that combines moving left, jumping, and shooting. at = {"move": "left", "vert": "jump", "attack": "shoot 135"}. (2) Both interfaces share the same visual observations and task objectives so that we can compare performance across levels of action abstraction. Timing modes. In real-time mode, the simulation continues during inference. In time-paused mode, it freezes during each decision and advances after receiving the action. Both interfaces use standard action interval of 0.2 seconds. Each action advances 0.2 seconds of simulation time in time-paused mode; in real-time mode, inference latency affects how often the agent acts. Two modes compare decision-making and execution under different time constraints. Difﬁculty and reward. Each encounter has ﬁxed Easy, Medium, and Hard parameter sets, calibrated as described in Section 3.4. All encounters use the same reward deﬁnition: given the bosss remaining health Ht in state st and its total health Hmax in the current conﬁguration, the step reward is rt = (Ht Ht+1)/Hmax. Evaluation reports average win rate and average progress: whether the boss is defeated and the fraction of its health removed, respectively (Section 4.1).

We add ﬁxed 200 ms delay to the controllers responses to approximate human reaction time. At higher difﬁculties, bosses deal more damage, have more health and skills, and are more likely to initiate attacks with less reaction time. Prior gameplay datasets have relied heavily on human recordings, which can include failed attempts and actions unrelated to the target task. These lower-quality demonstrations can hurt imitation learning. On Q*bert, behavior cloning on the top-scoring 5% of human episodes outperformed training on the full dataset (Kanervisto et al., 2020). Cleaning such recordings at scale takes substantial manual effort. Yue et al. (Yue et al., 2026) manually review ﬂagged clips and spot-check additional recordings, process that can still miss low-quality segments. We collect GAMEDOJO-Data by running the behavior-tree controllers in parallel. Once the controllers are in place, adding simulator instances increases collection throughput without recruiting more players. Each controller targets speciﬁc boss, so we can record demonstrations aligned with the encounter objective and verify episode outcomes from the game state. We collected 600 hours of trajectories for ﬁne-tuning across all 120 encounters and three difﬁculty levels, averaging 100 minutes per encounter and difﬁculty. GPT-6.1-Sol survives until the end in 47.6% and 1.7% of encounters in time-paused and real-time settings, showing that it can avoid boss attacks when having time to reason. The results show that GAMEDOJO remains far from saturation even in paused mode. Weaker models perform close to or below Random. Claude-Haiku-4.5 achieves 9.28% average PG in paused mode, only slightly above Randoms 7.66%, with zero WR. Under paused CUA, Qwen3.5-4B reaches just 1.94% PG, below Randoms 6.81%. Even GameScaling-9B-S3, generalist model pretrained on gameplay trajectories (Zhang et al., 2026a), reaches only 5.28% PG and zero WR in the same setting. Boss encounters remain challenging for smaller generalist models, even for those already trained on diverse gameplay. Most models make similar progress with Semantic and CUA. In paused mode, the median absolute PG gap between the two interfaces is 1.6 percentage points across the eleven frontier models. Gemini-3.8-Flash reaches 31.1% PG with Semantic and 21.0% with CUA, while GLM-5.3Flash reaches 23.4% with CUA and 18.9% with Semantic. All models fall below Random in real time. In real time, all evaluated models score below Random in PG and achieve zero WR. GPT-6.1-Sols average PG drops from 44.77% to 2.70%, while Opus-5.5 drops from 31.23% to 1.19%. In medium-difﬁculty CUA diagnostic with one episode per boss, switching from time-paused to real-time interaction reduces the mean number of recorded decisions per episode from 222.3 to 6.7 for GPT-6.1-Sol and from 229.1 to 5.4 for Claude-Opus-5.5. The sharp decline across both interfaces shows that acting effectively while the environment continues to change remains major challenge. The state-aware boss-speciﬁc script reaches 99.83% WR and 99.99% PG, showing the large gap to strong task-speciﬁc control.

sections.title: 4.3 Learning from Gameplay Trajectories
sections.content: After assessing frontier capabilities, we examine how trajectory supervision improves interactive performance. We obtain GAMEDOJO-4B by supervised ﬁne-tuning Qwen3.5-4B on 240 hours sampled uniformly from GAMEDOJO-Data: 40 minutes for each boss at each of three difﬁculty levels. Table 4 shows large gains from trajectory supervision across all three difﬁculty levels. In paused mode, GAMEDOJO-4B raises average PG from 3.04% to 42.92% and average WR from 0.09% to 21.39%. GAMEDOJO-4B reaches performance comparable to GPT-6.1-Sol: leading 0.83% in WR while losing 2.36% in PG, respectively. In real time, GAMEDOJO-4B achieves the best performance among all models at every difﬁculty level, reaching 26.26%, 8.18%, and 2.48% on easy, medium, and hard encounters. Across the three difﬁculty levels and both timing modes, the share of recorded decisions that pass CUA action format validation rises from 8.94%11.88% before SFT to 99.96%99.98% after SFT. These gains show that scripted gameplay trajectories therefore provide promising source of training data, and offers an effective way to improve interactive agents.

sections.title: 5.1 Performance across Difﬁculty Levels
sections.content: We examine the difﬁculty gradient across easy, medium, and hard conﬁgurations on the same tasks. Table 4 compares different models on all 120 bosses through CUA. Performance drops consistently with difﬁculty. PG decreases from easy to medium to hard for every evaluated model in both timing modes. For example, GAMEDOJO-4Bs paused PG falls from 76.70% to 40.32% and 11.75% and GPT-6.1-Sol falls from 78.08% to 44.59% and 13.17%. All reported model WRs on hard are zero in both modes, showing that the difﬁculty gradient extends to encounters that remain unsolved even after trajectory supervision. Real-time interaction remains demanding even on easy. On easy encounters, switching to real time reduces GPT-6.1-Sols PG from 78.08% to 13.65% and GAMEDOJO-4Bs from 76.70% to 26.26%. On hard encounters, the highest real-time PG among learned agents is only 2.48%, close to Randoms 2.31%. The boss-speciﬁc script reaches 35.83% WR and 93.23% PG under the same 180-second budget, exposing large gap to the privileged reference. Effective control under continuous environment changes remains challenging across difﬁculty levels. GameDojo: Benchmarking Real-Time Interactive Agents in Video Games

sections.title: 5.2 Learning and Transfer across Bosses
sections.content: We compare six-boss joint training and ﬁxed-source transfer in Terraria and Doom using PPO and SFT. The joint and single-boss runs use the same training budget per boss within each method (100K online steps for PPO and 2 hours of demonstrations for SFT). Joint training improves mean progress on individual bosses. At the ﬁnal checkpoint in Figure 4, six-boss joint PPO raises mean PG over separate training by 7.51 percentage points in Terraria and 26.46 in Doom. Across all twelve bosses, joint PPO raises mean PG from 47.7% to 64.7%. Joint SFT raises it from 69.5% to 87.5%. Single-boss training transfers within each game. We train on Queen Bee in Terraria or Cyberdemon in Doom and evaluate on the other ﬁve bosses in the same game (Figure 5). From initialization to the ﬁnal checkpoint, ﬁxed-source PPO raises mean PG by 34.96 percentage points in Terraria and 4.81 in Doom, going from 28.3% to 48.2% across the ten held-out bosses. sections.title: 5.3 Transfer across Games
sections.content: Fixed-source SFT reaches 73.65% mean PG on the other ﬁve Terraria bosses and 63.81% on the other ﬁve Doom bosses (Figure 5). We ﬁne-tune Qwen3.5-4B on GAMEDOJO-Data from one or six bosses in Terraria or Doom, or twelve bosses together. GAMEDOJO-4B provides the all-boss comparison. Figure 6 reports PG gains over Qwen3.5-4B for six model settings on ﬁve boss sets. Joint training yields the largest mean PG gains. Combining both games extends these gains beyond the source environments: joint SFT outperforms the four single-game variants in all ﬁve evaluation sets. PG improves by 15.39 and 14.48 percentage points on unseen 2D and 3D games, respectively, averaging 14.94 points over their 108 bosses. Transfer depends on the source environment. Both Doom-only models gain across all ﬁve groups, including unseen 2D games. Terraria-only models gain 4.195.77 points on other 2D games but lose 1.055.10 points on other 3D games. Adding Terraria bosses improves withingame performance without removing this directional difference, highlighting the value of diverse source environments for broader transfer. sections.title: Conclusion and Limitations
sections.content: Conclusion. We present GAMEDOJO, controllable and challenging interactive benchmark of 120 boss encounters across 20 games, together with the 600-hour GAMEDOJO-Data, the automatic data collection pipeline and the trajectory-supervised GAMEDOJO-4B. These resources support controlled studies of model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses for interactive intelligence. Limitations. Reconstructing encounters from videos, wikis and mechanics descriptions may omit implicit rules and visual details of the original games. Evaluation therefore measures performance in the reconstructed tasks; transfer to the original games and physical environments requires extra evaluation in those settings. Copyright and use. The encounters are independent reconstructions made for non-commercial scientiﬁc research only; game covers and screenshots are shown solely to identify the reference titles. During reconstruction, the models used public gameplay videos, wikis and descriptions of game mechanics as references and had no access to the original games source code. We did not reverse engineer or crack the original games. GameDojo research materials are for non-commercial use.

sections.content: (l) Genshin Impact (miHoYo, 2020). These third-person action RPG encounters alternate between avoiding attack patterns and closing in to deal damage. Changing phases, summons, and protected targets alter when the player can attack effectively. Bosses. Andrius (wolf lunges), Electro Hypostasis (exposed core), Maguu Kenki (phantom sword strikes), Oceanid (water summons), Ruin Guard (spinning automaton), Signora (ice and ﬁre phases). (m) Hexen II (Raven Software, 1997). In this ﬁrst-person fantasy action game, players aim at mobile targets while dodging spells and thrown weapons. Flying, mounted, and teleporting enemies change where the player needs to look next. Bosses. Airborne Bone Rider (aerial rider), Axe-Hurling Rider (thrown axes), Blinking Tether Rider (teleporting tether attacks), Boar Archer Rider (mounted archery), Orb-Warded Serpent (protective orbs), Star-Volley Sorcerer (star volleys). (n) Minecraft (Mojang, 2011). These ﬁrst-person sandbox encounters require players to track mobs in three dimensions and control their distance. Some enemies can be engaged at range, while others force the player to reposition before getting clear attack. Bosses. Ender Dragon (aerial passes), Iron Golem (heavy melee swings), Skeleton Archer (ranged arrows), Warden (sonic attack), Wither (explosive skulls), Zombie Leader (undead melee pressure). Table S1 lists each game, its viewpoint and genre, and all six boss encounters. A.2 Coding Agent Game Reconstruction Macro reconstruction workﬂow. We construct all 20 games from scratch using Claude-Opus-5.5 through Claude Code with max reasoning effort. For each target game, we gather public gameplay videos, wiki pages, and mechanics summaries, then run three stage workﬂow: 1. Speciﬁcation writing: The coding agent writes structured mechanics document covering player movement, attacks, cooldowns, resource rules, boss attack phases, hitboxes, visual cues, and win or loss conditions for all six bosses. 2. Engine and boss implementation: The agent implements the game simulation, arena geometry, boss state machines, and visual renderer using lightweight assets that keep combat cues readable without copying commercial ﬁles. 3. Three round veriﬁcation loop: Every new game passes three test and ﬁx rounds. Round 1 checks complete combat mechanics and boss phase transitions; Round 2 reviews visual clarity, attack warnings, and controls against reference material; Round 3 tests multi seed stability, exact replay, public Gym compliance, and frame rate. Any remaining bugs are ﬁxed and retested before game enters the benchmark. Gym packaging and rendering backends. All 20 games are exposed through single Gymnasium wrapper (reset(seed, options) and step(action)) that hides three lightweight runtime backends: (1) shared 2D Canvas engine (BB.Case) for 7 classic 2D games (Hollow Knight, Kirby, Terraria, KOF 97, Battle City, Cuphead, and Mega Man), (2) standalone browser based JavaScript engines for 12 games using HTML5 Canvas 2D (Touhou, Soul Knight, Isaac), CPU raycasting (Doom), or ofﬂine Three.js WebGL 3D (Sekiro, Genshin Impact, Quake II, Hexen II, Super Mario 64, Tomb Raider, Zelda: OoT, and NFS: Most Wanted), and (3) Python and NumPy simulation engine with headless hardware accelerated ModernGL perspective rendering for Minecraft. Visual effects and camera rendering read the simulation state without modifying physics or random number streams. For all 3D games, the wrapper enforces true perspective rendering and raises an error if hardware acceleration is unavailable, preventing software top down fallbacks from entering evaluation or training. The public interface returns only RGB frames and public control descriptions; internal health values, hitboxes, boss move tables, and reward veriﬁers stay hidden inside the environment wrapper. Fixed game parameters. Every environment shares the following ﬁxed runtime parameters: Resolution: 854 480 pixels (16:9), uint8 RGB array of shape (480, 854, 3). Simulation and rendering clock: Fixed 60 Hz tick rate (16.67 ms per tick), uniﬁed across all 20 games. Decision step: 200 ms per environment step (5 Hz), advancing 12 simulation ticks divided into 6 equal input substeps of 33.3 ms (2 ticks per substep). Episode limit: Hard engine timeout of 300 (18,000 ticks), ending early upon player death or boss defeat on the exact terminal tick. Determinism: Seeded pseudo random number generators and full engine state hashing guarantee bit exact replay given the same seed, difﬁculty, and action sequence. GameDojo: Benchmarking Real-Time Interactive Agents in Video Games 20 Step reward: Normalized boss health reduction per step, rt = (Ht Ht+1)/Hmax, with cumulative progress clipped to [0, 1] at episode end.

sections.content: A.3 Action Spaces Every environment supports two action interfaces over the same 200 ms decision step: uniﬁed Computer Use Agent (CUA) keyboard and mouse interface and game speciﬁc Semantic discrete interface. CUA action format. CUA action is single line token sequence specifying mouse motion and six 33.3 ms keyboard substeps for the next 200 ms: <action_start> ; K(1) ; . . . ; K(6) <action_end> Here X, [1000, 1000] are integer relative mouse displacements (X > 0 right, > 0 down), and [5, 5] is the scroll wheel delta (Z > 0 scroll up). Each substep K(m) (m = 1, . . . , 6) lists 0 to 4 simultaneously held controls separated by spaces from the shared 14-control set {W, A, S, D, Space, Shift, J, K, L, Q, E, R, LB, RB}, where LB and RB denote left and right mouse buttons. An empty substep releases all keys while keeping its semicolon separator. key appearing in consecutive substeps (or across adjacent 200 ms packets) remains continuously held rather than triggering fresh press; new press ﬁres only on released-to-held transition. Mouse motion follows one of three per game modes: None (mouse motion ignored), Pointer (2D crosshair movement normalized to screen coordinates), or Camera (3D yaw and pitch camera rotation). Semantic action format. Semantic action is multi-head discrete choice written as JSON dictionary mapping each action head to one named option, for example {"move": "left", "vert": "jump", "attack": "shoot 135"} in Terraria or {"move": "forward", "turn": "left_10", "attack": "fire"} in Doom. Any omitted head defaults to option 0 ("none"), and every combination translates deterministically into one 200 ms CUA packet (held across the full step). Across 19 games, heads are deﬁned in compact_actions.json such that separate heads never share keys or mouse axes and the total number of combinations stays strictly below 1,000. Terraria uses three-head layout (move vert attack = 3 3 19 = 171) covering 16 directional bow angles at 22.5 increments plus two sword swings. Malformed strings or out of range values in either interface execute neutral no op packet and increment the format error counter. Table S2 details both action spaces for all 20 games. sections.content: A.4 Scripted Controller Design Source aware controller synthesis. Because GAMEDOJO provides full access to each games source code, the coding agent writes dedicated behavior tree controller for every boss encounter. The agent reads the boss state machine, attack timers, projectile positions, player cooldowns, and the games legal CUA action space, then implements deterministic policy hook (exposed through BB.GAME.scripted, Module.scripted, or mc_scripted.scripted). Each controller observes live game state strictly in read-only mode, checked before and after every call by verifying that the engine state hash does not change. To keep demonstrations realistic and aligned with learned agents, every scripted controller runs at the same 200 ms decision step (introducing natural 200 ms reaction delay) and outputs only legal CUA action packets through the public Gym step function. In addition, we verify each games Semantic action space by snapping scripted CUA packets to the nearest Semantic action and conﬁrming that bosses remain winnable. Difﬁculty calibration from scripted controllers. We use the veriﬁed scripted controllers as consistent skill anchor to calibrate three difﬁculty levels per encounter. For each boss, the coding agent tunes numeric difﬁculty parameters such as boss health, movement speed, attack cooldown, projectile speed, and attack damage, then runs multi seed scripted evaluations until average clear times fall cleanly into three target bands: Easy (2030 s), Medium (4590 s), and Hard (150240 s). This procedure ensures that every difﬁculty tier reﬂects smooth progression in combat length and execution pressure while remaining reliably solvable by strong policy across random seeds. Two stage trajectory collection. We collect GAMEDOJO-Data from the scripted controllers using two stage parallel pipeline across all 120 bosses and all three difﬁculty tiers: 1. Headless rollout and ﬁltering: Parallel workers run the scripted controllers in headless symbolic mode (time_mode=paused) across distinct engine seeds to record actions.jsonl and replay.json. Only winning episodes that pass exact replay state-hash matching and basic engagement checks (movement ratio 0.05, at least 2 distinct key combinations, and at least 10 visited arena positions) are kept. 2. Replay rendering and dataset assembly: Accepted action traces are replayed tick-by-tick through the visual renderer to capture pre-action 854 480 RGB frames at 60 fps, encoded with H.264 (libx264, CRF 18, veryfast, yuv420p). Each video passes strict decode checks (exact frame count matching tick count, SHA-256 veriﬁcation, and zero corrupt or all-black frames). We remove duplicate action sequences by action-trace hash and partition episodes by (boss, seed) with zero cross-split overlap. The resulting GAMEDOJO-Data corpus contains 44,368 winning episodes totaling 604.6 h: 39,937 training episodes (543.9 h), 2,193 validation episodes (29.7 h), and 2,238 test episodes (31.0 h). B

sections.content: C.1 Benchmark Evaluation Protocol Time-paused vs. real-time modes. GAMEDOJO evaluates every environment under two timing protocols that share the exact same 60 Hz physics engine and 200 ms decision step: Time-paused mode (TP): The environment renders one 854 480 RGB frame and immediately freezes its 60 Hz clock while the agent runs inference. Only after the action arrives does the simulation advance by exactly one 200 ms step (12 ticks), after which it freezes again for the next observation. Inference speed therefore has zero effect on episode outcomes. Real-time mode (RT): The simulation clock stays coupled to wall clock inference time. If model call takes seconds from receiving the observation to returning an action, the environment ﬁrst advances by t/0.2 neutral no op steps (200 ms each, with all keys released and zero mouse displacement) before applying the returned action to the resulting state. Latency below 200 ms incurs zero lag steps. If the player dies or the boss is defeated during the no op lag steps, the episode ends on that exact tick and the late action is discarded. Evaluation forms across agent families. All three agent families are scored by the same encounter-level win rate (WR, %) and boss-health progress (PG, %), averaged ﬁrst over episodes within each boss and then with equal weight over all evaluated bosses: VLM and LLM agents: Receive 854 480 RGB frames, public control instructions, and 2 step sliding history of recent frames and actions. Frontier API models are evaluated on all 120 bosses with 300 step cap (60 game time) in TP mode and 180 wall clock budget in RT mode. Self-hosted Qwen3.5-4B and GAMEDOJO-4B checkpoints run 5 independent seeds per boss (600 episodes per difﬁculty and timing mode) with 180 (900 step) budget. PPO specialist policies: Receive only the current 84 84 grayscale frame with no text prompt or frame history, outputting Semantic actions at 0.2 steps up to the 300 engine limit. Each policy is evaluated for 20 episodes per boss using test seeds held out from training. Scripted controllers: State-aware behavior trees running through the same CUA step interface as privileged upper-bound reference, evaluated over 5 seeds per boss (600 episodes per difﬁculty) under matched 60 (300 step, TP comparison) and 180 (900 step, RT comparison) game-time budgets.
